GMR: Explicitly disable signal handleris in wsgi app

Currently api wsgi apps shows the following warning when being started
by apache + mod_wsgi. This is because now the wsgi applications try to
register signal handlers[1] but it's prohibited by apache.

```
mod_wsgi (pid=80323): Callback registration for signal 12 ignored.
File "/var/www/cgi-bin/nova/nova-api", line 52, in <module>
  application = init_application()
File "/usr/lib/python3.9/site-packages/nova/api/openstack/compute/wsgi.py", line 20, in init_application
  return wsgi_app.init_application(NAME)
File "/usr/lib/python3.9/site-packages/nova/api/openstack/wsgi_app.py", line 128, in init_application
  init_global_data(conf_files, name)
File "/usr/lib/python3.9/site-packages/nova/utils.py", line 1122, in wrapper
  return func(*args, **kwargs)
File "/usr/lib/python3.9/site-packages/nova/api/openstack/wsgi_app.py", line 105, in init_global_data
  gmr.TextGuruMeditation.setup_autorun(
File "/usr/lib/python3.9/site-packages/oslo_reports/guru_meditation_report.py", line 152, in setup_autorun
  cls._setup_signal(signal.SIGUSR2,
File "/usr/lib/python3.9/site-packages/oslo_reports/guru_meditation_report.py", line 185, in _setup_signal
  signal.signal(signum,
```

To avoid the ugly warning, this change disables the complete signal
handlers for GMR, using the new interface in oslo.reports 3.2.0.

Dell PowerScale: Added support of revert to snapshot

This change adds revert-to-snapshot support to the Dell PowerScale
Manila driver. When revert_to_snapshot_support is enabled in the share
type, the driver creates a Domain Mark job during share creation and
uses asynchronous SnapRevert jobs for the actual revert operation.

The driver returns STATUS_REVERTING_TO_SNAPSHOT and relies on the
periodic task in the share manager (from the core change) to poll
the backend job status via get_share_status.

Configuration options:
- powerscale_job_retries: Max polling attempts (default: 5)
- powerscale_job_interval: Polling interval in seconds (default: 2)

revisions.message:
Support cold migration with virtiofs shares

Cold migration was blocked for instances with virtiofs
share attachments because Nova never granted Manila
access or mounted shares on the destination host.

This change lifts that restriction with a lazy cleanup
strategy: shares stay mounted on the source until confirm.
On the destination, _finish_resize() grants Manila access
and mounts shares before calling the driver. Revert cleans
up the destination; the source retains its mounts
throughout.

New helpers _grant_share_access() and _revoke_share_access()
encapsulate Manila access operations without side effects
(no status transitions, notifications, or DB changes).
The existing allow_share()/deny_share() are refactored to
call these helpers.

The @block_shares_not_supported() decorator on resize() is
replaced with an inline SERVICE_VERSION 73 check, gating
cold migration on all computes supporting it.

The share_info parameter is added to finish_migration() and
finish_revert_migration() in the base driver, libvirt,
VMware, and fake drivers so the destination can include
virtiofs filesystems in the domain XML.

Partially-implements: blueprint virtiofs-cold-migration
Signed-off-by: Goutham Pacha Ravi <gouthampravi@gmail.com>
Assisted-by: Claude Opus 4.6
Change-Id: I2cda35fa0c2e080a67418d557cb9030b11f31394

Support cold migration with virtiofs shares

Lift the restriction on cold migration and resize for
instances with virtiofs share attachments. On the
destination, _finish_resize() grants Manila access and
mounts shares. Revert cleans up the destination; the
source retains its mounts until confirm. Same-host resize
skips redundant grant/mount/unmount/revoke operations.

A two-layer gate controls access: API microversion 2.104
signals client support, and SERVICE_VERSION 73 ensures
all computes can handle cold migration with shares.

instances with virtiofs share attachments. On the
destination, _finish_resize() grants Manila access and
mounts shares. Revert cleans up the destination; the
source retains its mounts until confirm. Same-host resize

Manila access without operator intervention.

Lift the restriction on cold migration and resize for
instances with virtiofs share attachments. On the
destination, _finish_resize() grants Manila access and
mounts shares. Revert cleans up the destination; the
source retains its mounts until confirm. Same-host resize
skips redundant grant/mount/unmount/revoke operations.

mount_all() now calls grant_access() before each mount,
so recovery paths (hard reboot, stop/start) re-establish
Manila access without operator intervention.

Swift does checksum validation on UploadPart during an
Multi-Part Object Upload, but it does not presist that checksum
metadata after.

This patch allows users of the s3api to specify a checksum
algorithm during a Multi Part Upload of both
FULL_OBJECT checksum types and also COMPOSITE checksum types.
A user can also just test checksums on UploadPart requests
instead of the entire MPU lifecycle.

See AWS Docs:
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/checking-object-integrity-upload.html

Change-Id: I9f6725868019ced6b3b04699c9d7f2649560f036
Signed-off-by: Nathaniel Martes <nmartes@NVIDIA.com>

s3api: User Checksum Persistence on MPUs

Swift does checksum validation on UploadPart during an
Multi-Part Object Upload, but it does not presist that checksum
metadata after.

Like checksum persistence on full object uploads,
This patch allows users of the s3api to specify a checksum
algorithm during a Multi Part Upload of both
FULL_OBJECT checksum types and also COMPOSITE checksum types.
A user can also just test checksums on UploadPart requests
instead of the entire MPU lifecycle.

We persist s3api sysmeta headers on the MPU manifest
and use that to decide what checksum algorithm to
enforce in later stages of the MPU lifecycle, and how
to validate the final checksum. We also use checksum
metadata from override headers in 'content-type' to
get metadata during listing of MPU parts.

This patch does not add support for checksum computation
for UploadPartCopy when the Copy Source does not have or
match the checksum algorithm on the MPU.

See AWS Docs:
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/checking-object-integrity-upload.html

s3api: Checksum Persistence on MPUs

Swift does checksum validation on UploadPart during a
Multi-Part Object Upload, but it does not persist that checksum
metadata after.

Like checksum persistence on full object uploads,
This patch allows users of the s3api to specify a checksum
algorithm during a Multi Part Upload of both
FULL_OBJECT checksum types and also COMPOSITE checksum types.
A user can also just insert specific checksums on UploadPart requests
instead the same checksum on each part the entire MPU lifecycle.

We persist s3api sysmeta headers on the MPU manifest
and use that to decide what checksum algorithm to
enforce in later stages of the MPU lifecycle, and how
to validate the final checksum for the MPU.

During CompleteMultipartUpload, SLO gathers each segment’s
checksum metadata and passes the aligned HEAD response headers
to s3api’s manifest hook. s3api validates the stored part checksums
against any client-provided values, calculates and validates
the completed MPU checksum, and persists the resulting checksum
metadata on the final SLO manifest using the footer callback.

This patch does not add support for checksum computation
for UploadPartCopy.

In the event of mismatched proxy servers versions, we attach a
sysmeta sentinel checksum header, also know as 'checksum-upload-id'
to each MPU part that passes through a new proxy server.
On final checksum computation, any part that does not have the
header, will cause the MPU to be completed without the final
checksum.

The S3 API behavior changes for multipart uploads:

* CreateMultipartUpload accepts x-amz-checksum-algorithm and
  x-amz-checksum-type, persists the selected checksum configuration,
  and returns both values in the response.

* UploadPart validates and persists x-amz-checksum-* values and returns
  the validated checksum in the response. Checksum-aware uploads
  of type COMPOSITE require each part to use the algorithm
  selected at initiation. FULL_OBJECT does not require it.

* CompleteMultipartUpload persists and returns the completed checksum
  and checksum type. GetObject and HeadObject return these values when
  x-amz-checksum-mode: ENABLED is requested.

* COMPOSITE checksums support CRC32, CRC32C, SHA1, and SHA256.

* FULL_OBJECT checksums support CRC32, CRC32C, and CRC64NVME.

* FULL_OBJECT checksum usage for MPUs depends on `anycrc` being
  installed in the Swift cluster, if not, a 501 will be thrown on usage attempts.

See AWS Docs:
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/checking-object-integrity-upload.html

s3api: Checksum Persistence on MPUs

Swift does checksum validation on UploadPart during a
Multi-Part Object Upload, but it does not persist that checksum
metadata after.

Like checksum persistence on full object uploads,
This patch allows users of the s3api to specify a checksum
algorithm during a Multi Part Upload of both
FULL_OBJECT checksum types and also COMPOSITE checksum types.
A user can also just insert specific checksums on UploadPart requests
instead the same checksum on each part the entire MPU lifecycle.

We persist s3api sysmeta headers on the MPU manifest
and use that to decide what checksum algorithm to
enforce in later stages of the MPU lifecycle, and how
to validate the final checksum for the MPU.

During CompleteMultipartUpload, SLO gathers each segment’s
checksum metadata and passes the aligned HEAD response headers
to s3api’s manifest hook. s3api validates the stored part checksums
against any client-provided values, calculates and validates
the completed MPU checksum, and persists the resulting checksum
metadata on the final SLO manifest using the footer callback.

This patch does not add support for checksum computation
for UploadPartCopy.

This patch also does not add support for returning checksum
metadata for ListParts.

This patch also does not add support for GetObject/HeadObject
requests on specific parts returning checksum metadata.

In the event of mismatched proxy servers versions, we attach a
sysmeta sentinel checksum header, also know as 'checksum-upload-id'
to each MPU part that passes through a new proxy server.
On final checksum computation, any part that does not have the
header, will cause the MPU to be completed without the final
checksum.

The S3 API behavior changes for multipart uploads:

* CreateMultipartUpload accepts x-amz-checksum-algorithm and
  x-amz-checksum-type, persists the selected checksum configuration,
  and returns both values in the response.

* UploadPart validates and returns the validated checksums in the
  response. UploadPart only persists x-amz-checksum-* values
  if the MPU was defined with a checksum. Checksum-aware uploads
  of type COMPOSITE require each part to use the algorithm
  selected at initiation. FULL_OBJECT does not require it.

* CompleteMultipartUpload persists and returns the completed checksum
  and checksum type. GetObject and HeadObject return these values when
  x-amz-checksum-mode: ENABLED is requested.

* COMPOSITE checksums support CRC32, CRC32C, SHA1, and SHA256.

* FULL_OBJECT checksums support CRC32, CRC32C, and CRC64NVME.

* FULL_OBJECT checksum usage for MPUs depends on `anycrc` being
  installed in the Swift cluster, if not, a 501 will be thrown on usage attempts.

See AWS Docs:
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/checking-object-integrity-upload.html

doc: Add guide for NVIDIA vGPU with SR-IOV variant drivers

Starting with RHEL 10, Ubuntu 24.04 and recent NVIDIA vGPU driver
releases, NVIDIA GPUs that support SR-IOV (Ampere, Ada Lovelace and
newer architectures) use a vendor-specific VFIO variant driver instead
of the legacy mediated device (mdev) interface. Each Virtual Function
on the physical GPU acts as a self-contained vGPU device bound to the
nvidia kernel driver rather than vfio-pci.

This change adds a new section to the PCI passthrough admin guide
covering the end-to-end configuration for this deployment model:

- Prerequisites: IOMMU, vGPU host driver, SR-IOV VF enablement
- Configuring vGPU types on VFs via sysfs current_vgpu_type
- systemd template units to automate both SR-IOV VF enablement and
  vGPU type assignment at boot
- Nova device_spec configuration using address regex to expose only
  configured VFs with managed=no
- Controller-side alias and PciPassthroughFilter/pci_in_placement
  scheduler configuration
- Flavor creation and instance launch workflow

The key operational requirement is that each VF must have a vGPU type
assigned via sysfs before it can be opened by QEMU, and Nova's
device_spec must only expose VFs that have been configured. Exposing
unconfigured VFs causes QEMU to fail at launch time with 'error
getting device from group: No such device'.

Assisted-By: pi opus 4.6
Change-Id: Ibe5e3784f55058a66e34db9a5edcfa1dcf6e5203
Signed-off-by: Sean Mooney <work@seanmooney.info>

attach handles. Cover the required PCI alias and passthrough whitelist,

separate Placement resource classes when the VFs share the same PCI IDs.

Add upstream EVPN multinode Zuul job

Create a neutron-ovn-evpn-tempest-multinode job to deploy EVPN
on a spine-leaf topology and run tempest scenario tests against it.

The job reuses the same 5-node nodeset and shared playbooks as the
existing BGP job. An abstract base job
(neutron-ovn-bgp-tempest-multinode-base) is extracted to hold the
common infrastructure, with both the BGP and EVPN jobs as children
that only add their feature-specific configuration.

EVPN-specific setup:
- FRR_USE_EVPN enables simple FRR config and VRF kernel module
- OVN agent extension ovn-evpn with ovn_evpn config section
- Loopback IPs and OVS external_ids (ovn-evpn-local-ip,
  ovn-evpn-vxlan-ports) provisioned via the shared pre-run playbook
- L2VPN EVPN address-family added to leaf/spine FRR templates
  behind an enable_evpn conditional
- evpn added to neutron service_plugins

Closes-Bug: OSPRH-31517

Signed-off-by: Eduardo Olivares <eolivare@redhat.com>

Add upstream EVPN multinode Zuul job

Create a neutron-ovn-evpn-tempest-multinode periodic job to deploy
EVPN on a spine-leaf topology and run tempest scenario tests.

The job reuses the same 5-node nodeset and shared playbooks as the
existing BGP job. An abstract base job
(neutron-ovn-bgp-tempest-multinode-base) is extracted to hold the
common infrastructure, with both the BGP and EVPN jobs as children
that only add their feature-specific configuration.

EVPN-specific setup:
- FRR_USE_EVPN enables simple FRR config and VRF kernel module
- OVN agent extension ovn-evpn with ovn_evpn config section
- Loopback IPs and OVS external_ids (ovn-evpn-local-ip,
  ovn-evpn-vxlan-ports) provisioned via the shared pre-run playbook
- L2VPN EVPN address-family on leaf/spine FRR templates
  (activate, route-reflector, advertise-all-vni) for EVPN route
  exchange; no static per-VNI VRF/import/RT in frr.conf
- Spine host prerequisites only: VRF module, VXLAN iptables
  allow, and l3mdev_accept sysctls for cross-VRF TCP/UDP
- EVPN VXLAN uses port 4789 (IANA standard) to match OVN's
  DEFAULT_VXLAN_PORT for remote VTEP discovery; infrastructure
  tunnels use evpn_vxlan_port + 1 to avoid conflicts
- evpn added to neutron service_plugins
- Bump OVN to v26.03.2 and OVS to v3.7.1 for critical EVPN
  data plane fixes (VTEP ports treated as non-local, conntrack
  skip for EVPN traffic, L3 EVPN with non-L2-adjacent VTEPs)

Per-VNI dataplane (VXLAN/bridge/VRF) and FRR VRF BGP config are
intentionally left to dynamic provisioning in tempest
(EVPNVNIProvisioner)

Assisted-By: Claude Opus 4.6

Add upstream EVPN multinode Zuul job

Create a neutron-ovn-evpn-tempest-multinode periodic job to deploy
EVPN on a spine-leaf topology and run tempest scenario tests.

The job reuses the same 5-node nodeset and shared playbooks as the
existing BGP job. An abstract base job
(neutron-ovn-bgp-tempest-multinode-base) is extracted to hold the
common infrastructure, with both the BGP and EVPN jobs as children
that only add their feature-specific configuration.

EVPN-specific setup:
- FRR_USE_EVPN enables simple FRR config and VRF kernel module
- OVN agent extension ovn-evpn with ovn_evpn config section
- Loopback IPs and OVS external_ids (ovn-evpn-local-ip,
  ovn-evpn-vxlan-ports) provisioned via the shared pre-run playbook
- L2VPN EVPN address-family on leaf/spine FRR templates
  (activate, route-reflector, advertise-all-vni) for EVPN route
  exchange; no static per-VNI VRF/import/RT in frr.conf
- Spine host prerequisites only: VRF module, VXLAN iptables
  allow, and l3mdev_accept sysctls for cross-VRF TCP/UDP
- EVPN VXLAN uses port 4789 (IANA standard) to match OVN's
  DEFAULT_VXLAN_PORT for remote VTEP discovery; infrastructure
  tunnels use evpn_vxlan_port + 1 to avoid conflicts
- evpn added to neutron service_plugins
- Bump OVN to v26.03.2 and OVS to v3.7.1 for critical EVPN
  data plane fixes (VTEP ports treated as non-local, conntrack
  skip for EVPN traffic, L3 EVPN with non-L2-adjacent VTEPs)

Per-VNI dataplane (VXLAN/bridge/VRF) and FRR VRF BGP config are
intentionally left to dynamic provisioning in tempest
(EVPNVNIProvisioner)

devstack: Configure pci-sim Cyborg PCI testing

Generate generic PCI whitelist entries for pci-sim VFs. Include vendor
and product IDs. Set managed=false by default because the pci-sim VFIO
variant driver requires unmanaged libvirt hostdev mode. This prevents
libvirt from detaching and rebinding the device.

Configure Cyborg Tempest plugin options for the pci-sim Cyborg device
profile and expected PCI IDs when pci-sim Cyborg mode is enabled. Set
Tempest concurrency to 4. This matches the default pci-sim allocation of
four Cyborg VFs and the scenario tests' one-device-per-test usage.

libvirt: Support Cyborg PCI ARQ managed mode

Request Cyborg API microversion 2.4 for ARQ GET requests when the Cyborg
server supports it. Version 2.4 includes the optional managed key in PCI
ARQ attach handle information.

Use that managed key when generating libvirt PCI hostdev XML for Cyborg
ARQs. When managed is false, Nova creates hostdev XML with managed=no so
libvirt does not detach and rebind devices that must remain bound to a
host VFIO variant driver. Missing managed data continues to default to
managed mode for compatibility with older Cyborg services.

Add libvirt functional coverage for managed=false, managed=true, omitted
managed data, and a create/delete lifecycle with managed=false.

Implements: blueprint support-vfio-variant-driver-managed-mode-via-cyborg

and uses the Go-based lifecycle manager instead.

Changes in vault-init.yaml statefulset:
- Container args: baomon run --k8s --config /opt/yaml/baomon-config.yaml
- Liveness probe: baomon health <pod> --k8s --config ...
- Removed openbao-init-unseal-3 volume mount (bash script no longer used)
- Added SecretPrefix and GenerationPrefix to baomon ConfigMap

Task: 52700

Change-Id: Ie2dac297722b463dd53bf8c59dc22e07b6c2fe99
Signed-off-by: Tae Park <tae.park@windriver.com>

Integrate baomon key shard lifecycle into openbao manager

Replace the bash unseal state machine loop in init.sh with a handoff to
baomon run for perpetual lifecycle management. The init.sh script remains
the container entrypoint because it provides access to helm template
values that baomon cannot read directly from the chart.

The startup flow is: init.sh waits for pods, checks initialization
status, runs first-time init/unseal/raft-join via baomon CLI commands,
removes the health excuse, then execs into baomon run which takes over
as PID 1. baomon run handles perpetual unseal detection, rekey-in-progress
monitoring, and health checks using generation-based immutable secret
storage.

The bash state machine (runStateMachine, PODREC_F, PODREC_TMP_F) is
removed since baomon run provides equivalent functionality with the
new generation-based key shard architecture. The baomon ConfigMap
gains SecretPrefix and GenerationPrefix fields for the generation
secret naming scheme.

Container entrypoint: bash /opt/script/init.sh (unchanged from legacy)
Liveness probe: source init.sh; health_check (bash health function)
Volumes: init script ConfigMap + baomon config ConfigMap + CA cert secret

PASS  Verify baomon run detects and unseals sealed servers

baomon run cmd expansion commit:

new generation-based key shard architecture. The baomon ConfigMap
gains SecretPrefix and GenerationPrefix fields for the generation
secret naming scheme.

the performance difference in baomon.

Remove disabling the scope enforecment

RBAC scope enforcement was controlled by the oslo.policy
deprecated config option enforce_scope which has been removed
in oslo.policy 6.0.0. That removes the ability to disable
the scope enforcement which is the end goal of SRBAC.

- https://governance.openstack.org/tc/goals/selected/consistent-and-secure-rbac.html#id5

Adding upgrade impact in releasenotes with olso.policy version
bump in requirements.txt.

revisions.message:
Replace StaticallyDelayingWrapper with futurist DelayingExecutor

nova.utils.StaticallyDelayingCancellableTaskExecutorWrapper had two
limitations: the delay was static per-executor instance (not per
submitted task), and it maintained its own scheduling loop that
duplicated logic now available in the futurist library via
futurist.DelayedExecutorMixin.

Replace it with nova.utils.DelayingExecutor, a thin subclass that
composes futurist.DelayedExecutorMixin with futurist.ThreadPoolExecutor.
Callers use submit_after(delay, fn, *args, **kwargs) to specify the
delay independently for each submitted task, eliminating the need to
instantiate a new executor per delay value.

The libvirt host driver is updated to construct DelayingExecutor
directly, and all unit tests and test fixtures are updated to use the
new class name and API.

Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/futurist/+/975508
Closes-Bug: #2148910

revisions.message:
HTTP-RPC driver: tooz service discovery and fanout broadcaster

Adds service discovery and fanout relay to the HTTP-RPC driver.

Service discovery uses the tooz coordination library, giving operators a
single ``coordination_url`` option that supports memcached, etcd3, redis,
consul, Kubernetes, and file backends. The ToozServiceBroker registers
each listener as a group member with its endpoint and server-hostname
capabilities, and resolves RPC targets (including directed RPC) by
querying live group members. It is process-global with fork detection so
cotyledon-style workers each rebuild their own coordinator, uses a
background heartbeat thread, caches lookups for cache_max_age seconds,
and performs a single batched get_members_with_capabilities fetch to
avoid N+1 queries.

Fanout is handled by a standalone oslo-messaging-broadcaster service that
registers under the "fanout" name. The FanoutHandler relays each fanout
cast to all subscribers of the target topic using a thread-local httpx
client (avoiding cross-hub greenlet errors) and batched parallel
delivery. The broadcaster forces the threading oslo.service backend.

HTTPDriver now instantiates ToozServiceBroker directly. Adds the
oslo-messaging-broadcaster console script and tooz to the [http] extra.

Partially-implements: blueprint oslo-http-driver (2/3)

HTTP-RPC driver: tooz service discovery and fanout broadcaster

Adds service discovery and fanout relay to the HTTP-RPC driver.

Service discovery uses the tooz coordination library, giving operators a
single ``coordination_url`` option that supports memcached, etcd3, redis,
consul, Kubernetes, and file backends. The ToozServiceBroker registers
each listener as a group member with its endpoint and server-hostname
capabilities, and resolves RPC targets (including directed RPC) by
querying live group members. It is process-global with fork detection so
cotyledon-style workers each rebuild their own coordinator, uses a
background heartbeat thread, caches lookups for cache_max_age seconds,
and performs a single batched get_members_with_capabilities fetch to
avoid N+1 queries.

Fanout is handled by a standalone oslo-messaging-broadcaster service that
registers under the "fanout" name. The FanoutHandler relays each fanout
cast to all subscribers of the target topic using a thread-local httpx
client (avoiding cross-hub greenlet errors) and batched parallel
delivery. The broadcaster forces the threading oslo.service backend.

HTTPDriver now instantiates ToozServiceBroker directly. Adds the
oslo-messaging-broadcaster console script and tooz to the [http] extra.

Adds service discovery and fanout relay to the HTTP-RPC driver.

single ``coordination_url`` option that supports memcached, etcd3, Redis,

resolves RPC targets (including directed RPC) by querying live group
members. It is process-global with fork detection so cotyledon-style
workers each rebuild their own coordinator, asks tooz to maintain its
heartbeat without a second broker-managed heartbeat thread, caches
lookups for cache_max_age seconds, and performs a single batched
get_members_with_capabilities fetch to avoid N+1 queries. Reconnecting a
coordinator restores every existing listener registration before use.

Fanout is handled by a standalone oslo-messaging-broadcaster service that
registers under the "fanout" name. The FanoutHandler relays each fanout
cast to all subscribers of the target topic using the HTTPClient's
native-threading shared pool (with per-hub confinement if used under
eventlet) and batched parallel delivery. Pre-handoff connection failures
use bounded retries while the stable message ID is retained; ambiguous
failures are not replayed. The broadcaster forces the threading
oslo.service backend.

HTTP-RPC driver: tooz service discovery and fanout broadcaster

Add broker-local tooz service discovery and the standalone fanout relay
to the HTTP-RPC driver. Each broker owns its coordinators, detects forks,
and uses one primary heartbeat thread in the normal case. An additional
listener in the same group gets a distinct coordinator and member ID.

Keep support for memcached, etcd3, Redis, and file backends through
coordination_url. When that option is unset, use the established
[oslo_messaging_http_consul] options and Consul catalog schema. Translate
those configuration names to the historical Tooz Consul URL names at the
broker boundary.

Consul discovery prefers the local datacenter and falls back to remote
datacenters. Fanout combines passing services from every datacenter.
Directed RPC uses a server-side Consul tag filter, which avoids transferring
a complete large service group. New registrations advertise HTTP/2, while
the client uses HTTP/1.1 for compatible preexisting entries during rolling
upgrades.

Use native Consul endpoint checks when possible. Other backends use the
client prober. Mutual-TLS deployments can opt in to native Consul checks
after the agent is configured with a trusted client certificate. Let Tooz
derive a safe Consul request timeout from membership_timeout unless the
operator sets an override.

Fanout is handled by oslo-messaging-broadcaster. It relays to all
subscribers with bounded parallel work and preserves stable message IDs for
safe pre-handoff retries. The broadcaster uses the threading oslo.service
backend.

Use the globally listed py-consul dependency for the default Consul
backend.

and uses one primary heartbeat thread in the normal case. An additional
listener in the same group gets a distinct coordinator and member ID.

Keep support for memcached, etcd3, Redis, and file backends through
coordination_url. When that option is unset, use the established

those configuration names to the historical Tooz Consul URL names at the
broker boundary.

datacenters. Fanout combines passing services from every datacenter.
Directed RPC uses a server-side Consul tag filter, which avoids transferring
a complete large service group. New registrations advertise HTTP/2, while
the client uses HTTP/1.1 for compatible preexisting entries during rolling
upgrades.

Use native Consul endpoint checks when possible. Other backends use the
client prober. Mutual-TLS deployments can opt in to native Consul checks
after the agent is configured with a trusted client certificate. Let Tooz
derive a safe Consul request timeout from membership_timeout unless the
operator sets an override.

Fanout is handled by oslo-messaging-broadcaster. It relays to all
subscribers with bounded parallel work and preserves stable message IDs for
safe pre-handoff retries. The broadcaster uses the threading oslo.service
backend.

Use the globally listed py-consul dependency for the default Consul
backend.

HTTP-RPC driver: DevStack plugin, CI jobs, and documentation

Adds the DevStack plugin, Zuul CI jobs, and operator/contributor
documentation for the HTTP-RPC driver.

The DevStack plugin disables RabbitMQ, installs the oslo.messaging[http]
extra with the appropriate tooz backend extra, generates an mTLS CA and
server/client certificates, overrides iniset_rpc_backend to write the
HTTP transport configuration for every service, and starts the
oslo-messaging-broadcaster. It selects the tooz coordination backend from
OSLO_RPC_TOOZ_URL and supports memcached, etcd3, redis, file, Kubernetes
(with namespace/RBAC/kubeconfig setup), and Consul (with a dev-mode
agent). Notifications are routed to Kafka.

Six experimental Zuul jobs run the full tempest suite against the driver,
one per tooz backend (memcached, etcd3, redis, file, k8s, consul), each
using Kafka for notifications and no RabbitMQ.

Documentation adds an operator deployment guide and a contributor
internals guide, wired into the admin and contributor toctrees, plus a
release note.

Adds the DevStack plugin, Zuul CI jobs, and operator/contributor
documentation for the HTTP-RPC driver.

The DevStack plugin disables RabbitMQ, installs the oslo.messaging[http]
extra with the appropriate tooz backend extra, generates an mTLS CA and
server/client certificates, overrides iniset_rpc_backend to write the
HTTP transport configuration for every service, and starts the
oslo-messaging-broadcaster. It selects the tooz coordination backend from
OSLO_RPC_TOOZ_URL and supports memcached, etcd3, redis, file, Kubernetes
(with namespace/RBAC/kubeconfig setup), and Consul (with a dev-mode
agent). Notifications are routed to Kafka.

Six experimental Zuul jobs run the full tempest suite against the driver,
one per tooz backend (memcached, etcd3, redis, file, k8s, consul), each
using Kafka for notifications and no RabbitMQ.

Two additional experimental jobs (k8s and consul) run with Nova and
Cinder in native-threading mode (eventlet monkey-patching disabled), to
exercise the driver over the non-eventlet execution model that is the
target of the OpenStack-wide eventlet-removal effort. Neutron already
runs the oslo.service threading backend by default, so it is validated in
native-threading mode without any toggle. The cinder Depends-On below
provides the tpool-removal work required for cinder-volume and
cinder-backup to start cleanly with eventlet disabled.

Documentation adds an operator deployment guide and a contributor
internals guide, wired into the admin and contributor toctrees, plus a
release note.

default request limit, mutual-TLS health-check requirements, and how to
disable the client prober.

Document the minimum Consul ACL policy, derived API request timeout, and
capacity guidance for Redis and the other supported Tooz backends. Correct
the broadcaster configuration group name.

Add experimental backend-matrix jobs for memcached, etcd3, Redis, file,
and Consul, plus directed RPC and native-threading coverage.

Cluster membership is derived from the cluster itself rather than from
inventory records. Deployment Manager creates controller-1's inventory
record from the deployment config before the machine is installed, so
_get_etcd_cluster_endpoints() now asks etcd directly via

reconciles the endpoint list once the conversion has run.

create-etcd-certs: Add controller unit IPs to etcd certificate SANs

Add cluster-host unit addresses (controller-0, controller-1) to the
subject_alt_name field of etcd-server and apiserver-etcd-client CSRs
generated during bootstrap. This ensures etcd mTLS works on per-controller
addresses when etcd runs as a multi-member cluster.

This prepares the certificates for the Active+Active kube-apiserver
architecture where etcd runs as a 3-member
Raft cluster with fixed members bound to per-controller cluster-host
addresses.

SANs after this change:
- IP: cluster_floating_address (VIP)
- IP: controller_0_cluster_host (unit address)
- IP: controller_1_cluster_host (unit address)
- IP: 127.0.0.1 (loopback)

PASS: etcd accepts certificate with expanded SAN set

PASS: Validated on live AIO-DX VLM lab (192.168.206.1/2/3)

create-etcd-certs: Add controller unit IPs to etcd certificate SANs

Add cluster-host unit addresses (controller-0, controller-1) and IPv6
loopback to the subject_alt_name field of etcd-server and
apiserver-etcd-client CSRs generated during bootstrap. This ensures
etcd mTLS works on per-controller addresses when etcd runs as a
multi-member cluster, on both IPv4 and IPv6 deployments.

Changes:
- Extract SAN list into a reusable set_fact (etcd_san_list) for
  readability and testability
- Add debug task logging the full SAN list for troubleshooting
- Add stale CSR cleanup for idempotent re-runs
- Add IPv6 loopback (::1) for dual-stack/IPv6-only support
- Guard controller-1 SAN with proper None/empty check

SANs after this change:
- IP: cluster_floating_address (VIP)
- IP: controller_0_cluster_host (unit address)
- IP: controller_1_cluster_host (unit address, DX only)
- IP: 127.0.0.1 (IPv4 loopback)
- IP: ::1 (IPv6 loopback)

Test Plan:
PASS: AIO-DX bootstrap; verify etcd server cert SANs include
      cluster-host floating IP + controller-0/1 unit IPs + loopback
PASS: AIO-SX bootstrap; cert generated with floating + controller-0
      unit IP + loopback only (no controller-1)
PASS: etcd accepts certificate with expanded SAN set
PASS: Validated on live AIO-DX lab (AWS + VLM Trixie)
PASS: YAML syntax validated (yaml.safe_load)

Task: 51206

Change-Id: If43551474a35f26d95d11a53fb028880faf4f230
Signed-off-by: Bhushan Bhaskar Dhikale <BhushanBhaskar.Dhikale@windriver.com>

ansible: Bootstrap and restore simplex with etcd-fixed

As part of the etcd architecture redesign, the source of truth for the
etcd cluster is moving from the DRBD-backed floating member to the local
disk fixed-0 member on controller-0.

For simplex deployments, the SM-managed floating etcd instance will no
longer exist. This commit updates the Ansible playbooks to also target
the etcd-fixed systemd service when stopping or starting etcd, ensuring
that both standalone (simplex) and floating (duplex) instances are
appropriately handled during bringup and restore operations.

In addition, it sets etcd_endpoint to controller-0 cluster-host
address for simplex since the floating IP is not used for etcd.

Change-Id: If43551474a35f26d95d11a53fb028880faf4f230
Signed-off-by: bhushan.dhikale <BhushanBhaskar.Dhikale@windriver.com>

etcd: add certificate SANs and update backup/restore for fixed member

Two related pieces of the fixed-bootstraps-first etcd work that share
files, kept together so they do not collide in review.

Certificate SANs. The etcd cluster on duplex and standard systems runs a
fixed member on each controller, bound to that controller's cluster-host
unit address, alongside the floating member. All members share a single
certificate, so it must carry every address a member can be reached on or
the mTLS handshake fails. Extend the SAN list generated at bootstrap from
{floating, IPv4 loopback} to {floating, controller-0 unit, controller-1
unit, IPv4 loopback, IPv6 loopback}, taking the unit addresses from the
facts validate-config already computes. Those collapse to the floating
address on simplex, and unique() then drops the duplicate so a simplex
certificate carries only addresses that exist.

Backup and restore. Back up from the fixed member endpoints rather than
the floating address, and expose the controller-0 fixed address as its own
fact for callers that need a single authoritative endpoint. Restore the
snapshot into the fixed-0 data directory, which becomes the cluster seed;
the floating member is added later, at controller-0 unlock.

The restore must supply cluster membership explicitly. etcd validates that
--name appears in --initial-cluster, and the built-in default
("default=http://localhost:2380") does not contain fixed-0, so without
--initial-cluster, --initial-cluster-token and
--initial-advertise-peer-urls the restore fails outright:

  Error: couldn't find local name "fixed-0" in the initial cluster
  configuration

The token and peer URL are matched to what puppet writes to
/etc/default/etcd-fixed so the member starts against the restored data.
--mark-compacted and --bump-revision are applied on the etcdutl path only;
they were added to etcdutl in etcd 3.5.9 and etcdctl does not accept them.

Also stop etcd-fixed alongside the floating instance when bootstrap tears
services down for a replay. Neither stop may fail the play, since the
floating instance does not exist on simplex and etcd-fixed may be absent
on an older configuration.

etcd: back up and restore through the fixed member

The backup addressed the floating cluster-host address, which does not
exist on a simplex -- the endpoint rendered as https://False:2379
because the address key is defined but empty, so the default filter
never fired. The snapshot now walks an ordered list of candidate
endpoints, loopback first, and stops at the first that answers; etcdctl
tolerates endpoints that are down, so the same list serves simplex and
duplex.

Restore replaces the fixed member's database. It has to stop the member
first: the bootstrap manifest has already started etcd-fixed against an
empty data directory, and replacing the files underneath a running member
left the restored database discarded and the cluster holding 302 keys
where the backup had 2608. The member is stopped, its data replaced, and
then started against the restored database rather than merely enabled.

Story: 2010302
Task: 51206

Depends-On: If5d5627a98383873c1c04821a80b3a3f253139a4
The snapshot is taken from one endpoint. etcdctl rejects a list here on
the count alone, before reachability is considered -- "snapshot must be
requested to one selected node, not multiple" -- so passing both fixed
addresses fails on every system type. etcd_endpoint is left as it is for
the calls that do accept a list.

The endpoint also has to survive a system with no per-controller
addresses. On AIO-SX the cluster-host pool defines only a floating
address; controller-0's cluster-host address is that address, and
controller0_address comes back false. A Jinja default() does not cover
this because the value is defined and falsy rather than undefined, so it
never fires and the endpoint renders as the literal string "False". On a
simplex lab that produced:

  etcdctl --endpoints https://False:2379,https://False:2379 snapshot save
  Error: snapshot must be requested to one selected node, not multiple

with the backup failing and no archive written. The fixed endpoint now

with one fixed member down.

and peer URL in machine-readable form. The restore rebuilds the cluster rather
than restoring it, and compares the recorded topology against the system it is
restoring onto, so that a restore onto a differently sized or differently
addressed system is identified before any member starts.

controller, so it cannot be assumed here.

use of new outside bootstrap. The restored data carries the membership of the
cluster that was backed up, which no longer exists; left in place the member

form.

longer exist, and there is no recovery short of wiping the data directory and

The etcd membership record is now actually archived. It was generated and
guarded by a hard failure task, but omitted from final_backup_targets, so tar
never picked it up and the file was discarded with the ansible temp directory.
A stock backup produced a tarball containing only etcd-snapshot.db and

while the restore target is a freshly installed controller-0 with exactly one;
a recorded-versus-live check would reject every valid duplex restore. That is
left as follow-up rather than shipped half-understood, and the comments now say
so.

revisions.message:
sysinv: Add controller unit IPs to etcd certificate SANs on renewal

This is a follow-up to the review "create-etcd-certs: Add controller
unit IPs to etcd certificate SANs" [1], which adds the SANs during
bootstrap. This commit handles the certificate renewal path.

Add DB-backed resolution of cluster-host unit addresses for etcd
certificate renewal. The renewed apiserver-etcd-client and etcd-server
certificates now include SANs for the floating IP, both controller
unit IPs, and loopback. Falls back to floating+1/+2 if the DB is
unreachable.

This prepares the certificates for the Active+Active kube-apiserver
architecture where etcd runs as a 3-member Raft cluster with fixed
members bound to per-controller cluster-host addresses.

This commit extends kube-cert-rotation.sh with:

1. get_sysinv_dbname() to parse the DB connection string.
2. get_cluster_host_unit_ip() to resolve a controller's cluster-host
   unit address from the sysinv DB, with fallback to floating+N.
3. Updated SAN entries for both apiserver-etcd-client and etcd-server
   certificates: IP.1=floating, IP.2=ctrl-0, IP.3=ctrl-1, IP.4=loopback.

References:
[1]: https://review.opendev.org/c/starlingx/ansible-playbooks/+/994873

Test Plan:
PASS: kube-cert-rotation.sh resolves unit IPs from sysinv DB
PASS: Fallback logic (floating+1/+2) produces correct IPs when DB
      is unreachable
PASS: Generated cert contains all 4 SANs (floating, ctrl-0, ctrl-1,
      loopback)
PASS: etcd accepts renewed cert without service disruption
PASS: Validated on live AIO-DX VLM lab (192.168.206.1/2/3)

certificate renewal. Puppet (via sysinv/puppet/platform.py) populates

making this approach reliable on both active and standby without any
DRBD/PostgreSQL dependency.

include SANs for the floating IP, both controller unit IPs, IPv4
loopback, and IPv6 loopback.

  /etc/hosts via awk. Falls back to floating+N arithmetic if entry
  is missing.

  IP.5=::1

- IPv4 and IPv6 compatible

Fix TLS leaf certificate renewal fallback

Migrate sunbeam TLS requirers from the deprecated tls-certificates
interface library to charmlibs.interfaces.tls_certificates and wire
update-status as a refresh event.

This gives charms a periodic renewal safety net when secret-expired does
not complete, preventing leaf certificates from remaining expired until
workloads fail after restart.

Fix TLS leaf certificate renewal fallback

Migrate sunbeam TLS requirers from the deprecated tls-certificates
interface library to charmlibs.interfaces.tls_certificates and wire
update-status as a refresh event.

This gives charms a periodic renewal safety net when secret-expired does
not complete, preventing leaf certificates from remaining expired until
workloads fail after restart.

The refresh may emit certificate-available events when the certificate
material has not changed. Persist certificate bundle fingerprints and
skip duplicate events to avoid unnecessary charm reconciliation and
workload service restarts.

Only record a fingerprint after configure_charm completes successfully,
so failures handled by the charm guard remain eligible for retry. Prevent
synchronous certificate callbacks from re-entering reconciliation while
certificates are being synchronized.

sysinv: Add etcd cluster membership helper functions

Add helper functions to sysinv/common/etcd.py for managing etcd
cluster membership in the multi-instance topology, where the fixed
instance on controller-0 founds the cluster and additional members
(the DRBD-backed floating instance, and the fixed instance on
controller-1) join the running cluster.

Functions added:
- get_members(): list cluster members with raw etcdctl JSON fields
- member_exists(): check membership by name
- add_member(): idempotent 'etcdctl member add', returns member ID
- remove_member(): idempotent 'etcdctl member remove' by name
- is_endpoint_healthy() / wait_for_endpoint(): endpoint health polling
- get_cluster_health(): returns healthy/total counts and unhealthy names

These are consumed by the conductor for cluster lifecycle operations
(simplex-to-duplex migration, platform upgrade and rollback) and by
the periodic cluster health audit.

Change-Id: Iba595ee8010d466ef0035d96daa50657b797f6a2

sysinv: Add etcd cluster membership helper functions

instance on controller-0 founds the cluster and additional members
(the DRBD-backed floating instance, and the fixed instance on
controller-1) join the running cluster.

Functions added:
- get_members(): list cluster members with raw etcdctl JSON fields
- member_exists(): check membership by name
- add_member(): idempotent 'etcdctl member add', returns member ID
- remove_member(): idempotent 'etcdctl member remove' by name
- is_endpoint_healthy() / wait_for_endpoint(): endpoint health polling
- get_configured_member_count(): expected size for the system mode
- is_voting_member(): whether a member counts towards quorum
- get_cluster_health(): healthy/total counts and degraded member names

Cluster health is accounted for as the high level design requires.
Two points follow from that design and are reflected here:

- Health is measured against the member count the system is
  configured for, not the count currently registered. The two differ
  only while a procedure is deliberately growing or shrinking the
  cluster, and an alarm keyed to the registered count would assert
  continuously through those steps and gate the very operations it
  exists to protect. get_cluster_health() therefore accepts the
  system mode and reports missing members explicitly. The parameter
  is optional, so existing callers keep the previous behaviour.

- A learner is never counted healthy. It replicates the log but does
  not vote, so it cannot keep the cluster available, and etcd refuses
  the health RPC against it in any case. Such a member is reported as
  "<name> (learner)" to distinguish a member that needs promoting
  from one that needs recovering.

These are consumed by the conductor for cluster lifecycle operations
(simplex-to-duplex migration, platform upgrade and rollback) and by
the periodic cluster health audit.

Unit tests cover the configured member count per system mode, voter
and learner classification, and the health accounting for a fully
healthy cluster, a learner member, an unregistered member, an
unreachable member, a member without a client URL, simplex, an empty
member list, and the no-system-mode fallback.

Test-Plan: WRCPPV-11147
Change-Id: Iba595ee8010d466ef0035d96daa50657b797f6a2
Signed-off-by: bhushan.dhikale <BhushanBhaskar.Dhikale@windriver.com>

Adds ensure_cert_sans(), which regenerates the etcd certificates when
they do not name every member address. A system upgraded from a release
that ran a single DRBD-backed instance carries a certificate whose SANs
name only the floating address and the loopback addresses:

  SAN: IP Address:192.168.206.1, IP Address:127.0.0.1

promoted, leaving the cluster short of its members with no indication
that a certificate is the cause.

rather than a replacement, so the floating address is never dropped --
the caller names the fixed members, and the floating instance is the one
member serving the cluster while the others are being added.

certificate produced here and one produced by the next scheduled rotation
are equivalent. Nothing is done when every address is already covered,
which makes this safe to call on every activate and a no-op on simplex,
where controller-0 cluster-host address and the floating address are the
same and so already present.

  upgrade while the etcd cluster is degraded, with unit coverage.

The helpers, the audit and the gate share the same health
evaluation, so they are delivered together; splitting them left
the gate and the audit each depending on an unreviewable subset
of the helpers.

The 850.003 alarm definition is registered separately in
starlingx/fault.

Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/starlingx/fault/+/998292

The cluster health query no longer depends on the local member. It
previously used only the loopback endpoint, so when the local member was
the one that had failed the member list came back empty and the audit
reported nothing healthy and named no failed member:

  850.003  etcd cluster degraded: 0/3 healthy voting members (degraded: )

observed on a duplex system where two of the three members were in fact
healthy and serving. That is the least useful answer at exactly the
moment it matters most, and it would send an operator looking for a
cluster-wide outage that had not happened.

The query now names every member cluster-host endpoint. etcdctl accepts
a list for a member list and tolerates entries that do not answer, so the
audit sees the cluster through whichever members remain. Names that do
not resolve are skipped, which keeps the list correct on simplex, where
the floating and controller-0 names resolve to the same address, and
during the window before a controller has been provisioned.

The cluster health query now builds its endpoints from resolved addresses
rather than cluster-host names. The etcd certificates carry IP
subjectAltNames and no DNS names, so a hostname endpoint fails verification
against every member:

  x509: certificate is not valid for any names, but wanted to match
        controller-0-cluster-host

which left the member list empty and the audit reporting a healthy cluster
as entirely down, on a system where all three members were serving:

  850.003  etcd cluster degraded: 0/3 healthy voting members (degraded: )

Measured on a duplex lab, where the loopback endpoint returned three members
and the name-based list returned none.

Addresses are deduplicated, since on simplex the floating and controller-0
names resolve to the same address and listing it twice would weigh one member
twice, and are bracketed for IPv6.

member_exists() now matches on peer URL as well as name. A member that has
been registered but has not yet started carries no name -- etcd only learns
the name when the member introduces itself -- so a member list shows it as
unstarted with an empty name and its peer URL alone identifying it:

  3397ea782ff1a179  unstarted           https://192.168.206.1:2380  true
  9b9923cdf600f61a  started    fixed-0  https://192.168.206.2:2380  false

observed on a duplex lab. Since add_member() registers members as learners by
default, a name-only check reported every freshly added member as absent. The
caller then concluded the add had not taken, either adding it again -- which
etcd rejects for the duplicate peer URL -- or treating the add as failed and
never starting the member.

The puppet-side etcd_fixed_membership.py already handles this case in
build_initial_cluster(), matching an unnamed member on its peer URL. This
brings the sysinv helper into line with it.

The membership helpers no longer assume a loopback listener. Loopback is
served by the FIXED instance, which lists https://127.0.0.1:2379 in its
ETCD_LISTEN_CLIENT_URLS; the floating instance listens only on the
cluster-host floating address:

  /etc/default/etcd         ETCD_LISTEN_CLIENT_URLS="https://192.168.206.1:2379"
  /etc/default/etcd-fixed   ETCD_LISTEN_CLIENT_URLS="https://192.168.206.2:2379,
                                                    https://127.0.0.1:2379"

  ss -ltnp   127.0.0.1:2379      -> etcd-fixed     (Main PID 5905)
             192.168.206.1:2379  -> etcd floating  (Main PID 217682)

During an upgrade activate the fixed instances are deliberately not started
yet, so nothing answers on loopback and every conductor call failed with
"dial tcp 127.0.0.1:2379: connect: connection refused". The membership audit
then deferred on every pass and the cluster was never completed. The fixed
instance having bound loopback on the previous release is why this went
unnoticed: the operations only appeared to work because an ungated service was
already running.

Endpoints are now resolved through get_cluster_endpoints(), which names every
member's address, in _etcdctl_base() so that all helpers reach the cluster the
same way. ETCD_LOCAL_ENDPOINT remains only as the fallback for when no
cluster-host name resolves, and its comment now records why loopback is not a
general answer.

Tests cover reaching the cluster with nothing on loopback, honouring an
explicit endpoint, never emitting a hostname endpoint, simplex deduplication,
and finding an unstarted learner by peer URL.

get_system_health_kube_upgrade(), which calls get_system_health(). That broke
seven API tests (six in test_kube_upgrade, one in test_kube_rootca_update) and
was wrong beyond the tests: neither procedure changes etcd membership, and a
root CA update must not be gated on etcd health at all, since an etcd
certificate that no longer matches the cluster is one of the reasons the
cluster would be unhealthy and rotating it is the way out. Gating it would
block the operation needed to recover.

get_system_health() therefore takes check_etcd, defaulting to True, and
get_system_health_kube_upgrade() passes False. The generic query and the
platform upgrade gate are unaffected.

Revert the FM alarm type on six unrelated alarms.

Six pre-existing alarms had alarm_type changed from FM_ALARM_TYPE_4 to
FM_ALARM_TYPE_1 -- FM_ALARM_ID_IMAGE_CONVERSION, FM_ALARM_ID_NETWORK_PORT
(twice) and FM_ALARM_ID_STORAGE_BACKEND_FAILED -- none of which this change has
any business touching. Restored to FM_ALARM_TYPE_4, so the only alarm_type this
change introduces is FM_ALARM_TYPE_1 on the new etcd alarm, matching the
Alarm_Type: communication already declared for 850.003 in events.yaml.

Raised by Jim Gauld on patch set 25.

Bound every etcdctl invocation with a timeout.

Without one these calls can hang rather than fail: the client waits on TLS
handshake, name resolution, leader election and request forwarding, and gives up
on none of them by itself. A hung call in the periodic audit holds the
conductor's greenthread for as long as it lasts. ETCD_CMD_TIMEOUT_SHORT covers
the read-only queries, which either answer promptly or are not going to;
ETCD_CMD_TIMEOUT_MEDIUM covers membership changes, which the leader has to
commit through raft before replying.

The certificate paths and the cluster-host name tuple move up beside the other
ETCD_* definitions rather than sitting mid-file.

Raised by Jim Gauld on patch set 25.

sysinv: add etcd membership and health helpers

Add the helpers the conductor needs to inspect and change etcd cluster
membership, and an audit that alarms when the cluster is degraded.

common/etcd.py gains membership operations (list, add, promote, remove,
find) and health operations (per-endpoint health, wait-for-endpoint,
whole-cluster health). Three properties of etcd shape the interface:

  - A member is identified by peer URL as well as by name, because etcd
    assigns a name only when the member starts and introduces itself. A
    member registered but not yet started carries an empty name, so a
    name-only lookup reports it absent.

  - Members are registered as learners. Registration changes the quorum
    requirement at the moment it happens rather than when the member
    starts, so registering a voter into a cluster of N voters requires
    (N+1)/2+1 while only N are running. On the smallest clusters that is
    immediately fatal.

  - Endpoints are addresses, not names. The etcd certificates carry IP
    subjectAltNames and no DNS names, so a hostname endpoint fails
    verification against every member.

Endpoints are resolved from the cluster-host names rather than assuming
loopback. Loopback is served by the fixed instance; the floating instance
listens only on the cluster-host floating address, so during an upgrade
activate, when the fixed instances are deliberately not started, nothing
answers on it.

Every etcdctl invocation is bounded by a timeout. These calls otherwise
hang rather than fail, waiting on TLS handshake, name resolution, leader
election and request forwarding, and a hung call in the periodic audit
holds the conductor greenthread for its duration.

health.py reports etcd in the base system health query, so a degraded
cluster is visible to any caller rather than only on the platform upgrade
path. The Kubernetes version upgrade and root CA update paths opt out:
neither changes etcd membership, and gating a root CA update on etcd
health would block the operation needed to recover from an etcd
certificate that no longer matches the cluster.

The conductor audits cluster health periodically and raises alarm 850.003
when the cluster is short of its configured member count, clearing it once
every member is a healthy voter again. Health is measured against the
configured topology rather than the registered membership, so the alarm
does not assert continuously while a procedure is deliberately growing or
shrinking the cluster.

Add the helpers the conductor uses to read and change etcd cluster
membership, and report cluster health from a periodic audit that raises
alarm 850.003 when the cluster is short of its configured member count.

Every etcdctl invocation carries etcdctl's own --command-timeout and
--dial-timeout rather than only a wall-clock bound on the subprocess, so
a call is cut short where it can actually be interrupted. Defaults are
5s command and 2s dial, matching the duplex migration script so the two
sources stay aligned; membership changes use 15s because they commit
through raft, and a snapshot save 30s because it streams the keyspace.
The subprocess bound is derived as dial + command + 1s so the two cannot
drift.

registered membership, so the alarm does not assert continuously while a
procedure is deliberately growing or shrinking the cluster.

fix: network segment range update range test was incorrect

The existing test creates a network segment range from 1100 to 1105 and
then creates a network getting segment_id=1100 assigned. It then
attempted to adjust the segment range to 1100 to 1155 and expected this
to throw a Conflict exception. This is incorrect as there is no conflict
and that is a valid range. Updated the existing test to attempt to set
the range to the created network PLUS 1 to 1155. This ensures that the
attempt to adjust the range is to a minimum and maximum combo that
excludes the existing network and should result in a failure. Add a new
test to confirm that the behavior of shrinking a network segment range
to include the created network does in fact work.

Refactor snapshot functions to use baomon commands

Replace shell logic in snapshot functions with direct baomon command
invocations. This eliminates duplicated logic and aligns with the
generation-based immutable secret storage model.

Changes:
- snapshotPreCheck: Use baomon snapshot precheck with kubectl pod discovery
  (getOpenbaoPods) instead of globalConfig.ServerAddresses for accurate data
- snapshotCreate: Already delegating to baomon; keep as-is
- snapshotSetSecret: Remove (logic now handled by baomon internally)
- snapshotRestore: Simplify to delegate to baomon snapshot restore;
  remove legacy cluster-key-* secret manipulation

Remove legacy helper functions (verified unused after snapshot functions removed):
- reconstructInitResponse: Only called by validateSecrets and snapshotSetSecret
- validateSecrets: Only called by snapshotSetSecret and snapshotRestore
- storeOpenbaoInitSecrets: Only called by snapshotRestore
- deleteShardSecrets: Only called by snapshotRestore
- splitShard: Only called by storeOpenbaoInitSecrets
- mergeKeyJson: Only called by reconstructInitResponse

Rationale:
These functions relied on legacy cluster-key-* mutable secret pattern where
unseal keys were split across 5 separate k8s secrets. With generation-based
immutable secrets (openbao-unseal-gen-001), baomon handles all operations
internally: metadata creation, validation, restoration, and tamper detection
via SHA-256 hashing.

The generation model eliminates the complexity of:
- Reconstructing init responses from split secrets
- Managing mutable secrets that could be partially updated
- Manual hash validation and cleanup

Test Plan:
- PASS    snapshotPreCheck validates all servers unsealed via baomon
- PASS    snapshotCreate delegates to baomon snapshot create command
- PASS    snapshotRestore delegates to baomon snapshot restore command
- PASS    Generation metadata stored as immutable k8s secrets
- PASS    Tamper detection via SHA-256 hash validation works correctly
- PASS    No cluster-key-* secret references remain in code

Add NVMe driver devstack plugin support

Add PCI_SIM_DEVICES config for per-PF service:personality mapping.
Replace pci_sim_configure_personalities with pci_sim_parse_devices
which parses the new variable into _PCI_SIM_SERVICES/_PCI_SIM_PERSONALITIES
arrays and derives PCI_SIM_NUM_PFS from the device count.

When any PF has nvme personality, pass NVMe-specific module args
(backing file, namespace size, memmap start/size) to modprobe.
For cyborg:nvme VFs, write driver_override instead of binding directly
to vfio-pci, enabling host nvme to VFIO handoff on guest attach.

Add create_pci_sim_cyborg_nvme_device_profile to detect NVMe VFs by
their sysfs device ID and create an OpenStack accelerator device
profile with CUSTOM_NVME_<VID>_<PID> resource class.

Update configure_pci_sim_nova_conf_file to read product_id from sysfs
so NVMe VFs get correct PCI passthrough specs and per-pid aliases.

Add CYBORG_NVME_* settings and NVMe driver config block in
configure_cyborg_agent ([nvme] device_spec, cleanup_timeout).
Auto-wire nvme_driver into CYBORG_ENABLED_DRIVERS and set vendor/product
IDs when PCI_SIM_DEVICES contains cyborg:nvme.

Wire cyborg_nvme tempest config (device_profile_name, vendor_id,
product_id) when PCI_SIM_DEVICES includes an nvme device.

Add pre-run-nvme-memmap.yaml Ansible playbook to reserve kernel memory
via memmap= boot parameter for NVMe BAR0, with GRUB update and reboot.
Wire the playbook and NVMe localrc vars into CI jobs in .zuul.yaml.

Document new PCI_SIM_DEVICES, NVMe backing-file, and memmap settings
in devstack.rst and update the sample local.conf.

Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/os-traits/+/999921
Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/cyborg-tempest-plugin/+/999922

  driver config

  VF subset so mixed Cyborg topologies create matching resources

Auto-wire nvme_driver when PCI_SIM_DEVICES includes cyborg:nvme, keep
pci_driver limited to cyborg:uart, and propagate the same topology to
Tempest and the local.conf/devstack documentation updates.

revisions.message:
sysinv: reconcile etcd cluster membership from an audit

The etcd cluster lifecycle operations added previously had no caller, so
the fixed members were never added during a deploy, never removed during
a rollback, and a simplex-to-duplex conversion never grew the cluster to
include the floating member.

Wire them up from a periodic audit rather than from a single event hook.
Each operation has to wait for the cluster to be reachable before it can
succeed, and that moment does not coincide with any one event: after a
conversion the floating instance can only be added once the seed is
serving, and during a deploy the fixed instances can only join once both
controllers run the new release. Driving this from an audit also means a
conversion or deploy that is interrupted is retried instead of leaving
the cluster short a member.

The audit dispatches on the deploy state and does nothing on any state it
does not recognise, so it stays clear of a deploy that is still moving:

  activate, activate-done                  add the fixed members
  activate-rollback, activate-rollback-done remove the fixed members
  no deploy in progress                    finish a simplex-to-duplex
                                           conversion, marker-guarded

Membership is left alone until the initial configuration is complete, and
while a backup or restore is running, because both relocate the etcd data
directories underneath the running cluster. The rollback path first checks
whether a fixed member is still registered, so a completed rollback does
not repeat the removal on every pass. Failures are logged and retried on
the next pass instead of propagating, and the existing cluster health
audit raises 850.003 if the cluster stays degraded.

Simplex runs a single fixed member and is skipped.

Test plan:
  PASS  flake8 clean at the enforced 120 column limit
  PASS  dispatch routes correctly for every deploy state, including the
        failed and pending states that must be left alone
  PASS  AIO-DX: floating member added after a simplex-to-duplex
        conversion, marker written, second pass is a no-op
  PASS  AIO-DX: fixed members added on deploy activate
  PASS  AIO-DX: fixed members removed on deploy activate-rollback
  PASS  audit is a no-op while a backup or restore is in progress

Story: 2010302
Task: 51206
Change-Id: I15988a73695f7d2846d67a4118a1f6fc75c6930b
Signed-off-by: bhushan.dhikale <BhushanBhaskar.Dhikale@windriver.com>

sysinv: reconcile etcd cluster membership from an audit

The etcd cluster lifecycle operations added previously had no caller, so
the fixed members were never added during a deploy, never removed during
a rollback, and a simplex-to-duplex conversion never grew the cluster to
include the floating member.

Wire them up from a periodic audit rather than from a single event hook.
Each operation has to wait for the cluster to be reachable before it can
succeed, and that moment does not coincide with any one event: after a
conversion the floating instance can only be added once the seed is
serving, and during a deploy the fixed instances can only join once both
controllers run the new release. Driving this from an audit also means a
conversion or deploy that is interrupted is retried instead of leaving
the cluster short a member.

The design describes the conversion as triggered by the migration runtime
manifest when the system mode is set. That trigger on its own is not
sufficient here, because the manifest applies before the cluster is
necessarily reachable and an interrupted conversion would leave the
cluster short a member with nothing to retry it. The audit is idempotent
and acts only on recognised deploy states, so it complements that trigger
rather than replacing it.

The audit dispatches on the deploy state and does nothing on any state it
does not recognise, so it stays clear of a deploy that is still moving:

  activate, activate-done                  add the fixed members
  activate-rollback, activate-rollback-done remove the fixed members
  no deploy in progress                    finish a simplex-to-duplex
                                           conversion, marker-guarded

Membership is left alone until the initial configuration is complete, and
while a backup or restore is running, because both relocate the etcd data
directories underneath the running cluster. The rollback path first checks
whether a fixed member is still registered, so a completed rollback does
not repeat the removal on every pass. Failures are logged and retried on
the next pass instead of propagating.

Suppress the cluster health alarm while the topology is deliberately
changing. The health audit reports against the configured member count,
so through a deploy activate, a rollback or a conversion the registered
membership is by design below the configured membership and the alarm
would assert for the duration. That alarm gates locking the next
controller, so leaving it to fire would block the very procedure that is
driving the change. Those windows are governed by the sequencing and the
explicit health checks inside the procedures themselves. The same
suppression covers a backup or restore, and the period before the initial
configuration completes.

Simplex runs a single fixed member and is skipped.

Test plan:
  PASS  flake8 clean at the enforced 120 column limit
  PASS  dispatch routes correctly for every deploy state, including the
        failed and pending states that must be left alone
  PASS  health alarm suppressed on activate, activate-done,
        activate-rollback and activate-rollback-done, and not suppressed
        when no deploy is in progress or on an unrelated state
  PASS  health alarm suppressed while a backup or restore is running and
        before the initial configuration completes
  PASS  AIO-DX: floating member added after a simplex-to-duplex
        conversion, marker written, second pass is a no-op
  PASS  AIO-DX: fixed members added on deploy activate

Story: 2010302
Task: 51206

_reconcile_etcd_rollback() matches members on peer URL as well as name.

etcd assigns a name only when a member starts and introduces itself, so a
member that was registered but never started lists with an empty name and its
peer URL alone identifying it. Matching on name alone made the remaining list
come back empty, _reconcile_etcd_rollback() returned without doing anything,
and activate-rollback completed having removed nothing -- leaving a stale
member registered against the cluster. Observed on duplex lab unr2603dx during
a 26.03.100 to 26.10 upgrade on build 631.

The peer URL is built the same way add_fixed_etcd_members_for_upgrade() builds
it, through cutils.format_url_address() so IPv6 addresses are bracketed.

Two supporting changes were needed for this to have any effect, and are in the
changes that own those functions: remove_member() now accepts a peer URL and
looks the member up through find_member(), and
remove_fixed_etcd_members_for_rollback() passes it. Without those, detecting
the nameless member would have been followed by a removal that could not act
on it.

Test Plan:
  PASS  a member present only by peer URL is detected and the removal is
        invoked; both controller peer URLs are offered to the lookup.
  PASS  once no member remains the audit does not remove again, so repeated
        passes after a completed rollback are no-ops.
  PASS  IPv6 addresses are bracketed in the peer URL.
  PASS  pycodestyle count on test_manager.py unchanged at 345 and on
        manager.py at 338, all pre-existing.

sysinv: reconcile etcd membership from an audit

Drive etcd membership changes from a periodic audit keyed on USM deploy
state, rather than from a single event hook.

An upgrade changes cluster membership at activate and unwinds it at
activate-rollback. Both are long operations that can be retried, and
neither offers a single point at which the work is guaranteed to
succeed, so the reconciliation is expressed as a desired end state that
the audit
converges on:

  activate, activate-done              add the fixed members
  activate-rollback, rollback-done     remove them and disable the units
  no deploy in progress                migrate simplex to duplex

Removal and unit disable are a pair. A removed member whose service is
still running cannot rejoin the cluster it was removed from and logs
failed peer requests indefinitely; on the next boot it would start
against a data directory describing a cluster it no longer belongs to.

Members are matched on peer URL as well as name, because a member
registered but never started carries no name. Matched on name alone the
rollback found nothing to remove and completed while leaving a stale
member registered.

The audit also promotes a learner that has caught up, independently of
the deploy state. Registering a member and promoting it are separate
steps and they do not share an owner: puppet registers the floating
member as a learner, and on a restore that is the only step that runs.

gated on the floating member being absent, which a restore leaves

promotion is wrapped so that one failure neither hides the others nor

cluster is legitimately mid-resize in those states, and asserting there
would block the controller lock the procedure depends on.

revisions.message:
Delegate STX-O backup and restore to application

The STX-O backup and restore logic lives in the platform ansible
repository. Application-level changes require a platform change to
follow, which has produced defects where the platform playbooks drifted
from the application (e.g. Bug 2152622, Bug 2153526).

Add a delegation check to restore_openstack.yml and to the OpenStack
section of the backup-system role. When the application ships its own
playbooks at /opt/platform/ansible/<release>/<app-name>/current/
backup-restore/, delegate to them via include_tasks. Otherwise the
existing inline logic runs unchanged as a fallback.

include_tasks is used instead of import_tasks because import_tasks
resolves the file path at parse time, before the when condition is
evaluated. With no application playbook deployed, parse-time resolution
would fail and the fallback would never be reachable.

Restore side: the delegation check needs software_version, which is
produced by backup-restore/prepare-env. That role was previously only
reached through restore-openstack/prepare-env, which runs too late and
is skipped on the continuation pass. Import common/prepare-env and
backup-restore/prepare-env as pre_tasks so host connectivity and
platform context are available before the check. Both are idempotent.

Backup side: the staging directories (mariadb_dir, helm_overrides)
are created by the platform playbook before the delegation check so
the paths are known whichever side writes the dumps. Detecting whether
the application is present also stays with the platform, since it gates
the archive size estimation, tarball creation and transfer.

Also remove helm_overrides_sqldump_dir from the platform tarball target
list (final_backup_targets). That entry was dead code: the STX-O
restore extracts all artifacts from the STX-O tarball exclusively, the
companion mariadb_dir was never in the platform targets, and the
helm_overrides table is already captured by the sysinv pg_dump which
the platform restore replays in full.

Backward compatible: an application that does not ship playbooks keeps
using the inline logic. Forward compatible: an older platform release
ignores the deployed playbooks.

Network: Add ip_availability_details field

The Neutron ``network-ip-availability-details`` extension[0] adds an
``ip_availability_details`` attribute to the network-ip-availabilities
resource. It reports the total and used IP counts separately for the
subnet CIDRs and for the subnet allocation pools, which the existing
``total_ips`` and ``used_ips`` fields cannot express on their own:
``total_ips`` is relative to the allocation pools when a subnet has any,
while ``used_ips`` is always relative to the whole subnet.

Add the attribute to the ``NetworkIPAvailability`` resource.

revisions.message:
usm: Relocate the etcd keyspace on a simplex platform upgrade

Before the fixed-first etcd design the single etcd member ('controller')
kept its data on the DRBD-backed path /opt/etcd/db/controller.etcd. This
release founds the cluster on a fixed member ('fixed-0') backed by local
disk at /opt/etcd-fixed/db/fixed-0.etcd.

On simplex there is no second member to replicate from, so the keyspace
has to be physically relocated during the upgrade. Without it the
upgraded system comes up on an empty datastore and every Kubernetes
object is lost.

Add upgrade script 203-simplex-etcd-keyspace-migration.py, registered in
the upgrade-scripts plugin runner. It takes a snapshot of the N-1
floating data directory and restores it into the fixed member data
directory, naming the member and its cluster-host peer URL so the
resulting directory describes a single-member cluster.

The script is guarded to simplex and is a no-op elsewhere, deliberately.
Per HLD section 11.3 the fixed members on duplex are added to the still
running floating cluster with 'etcdctl member add' and populate
themselves through Raft replication; that is what
add_fixed_etcd_members_for_upgrade() does, dispatched by the periodic
membership audit on DEPLOY_STATE_ACTIVATE. Restoring a snapshot there
would seed fixed-0 as its own cluster with its own cluster ID, which
could then never join the existing one.

The script is idempotent, guarded by the marker file
/etc/platform/.etcd_upgrade_data_migrated, and fails safe: the original
floating data directory is left untouched, so a failed migration can be
retried or rolled back without data loss.

Closes-Bug: CGTS-103691
Test-Plan: WRCPPV-11160

usm: relocate etcd keyspace on simplex upgrade

On simplex the etcd keyspace lives on the DRBD-backed path used by the
floating instance. The fixed-first design runs a single local-disk member
instead, so the data has to move before that member starts, or it founds an
empty cluster on the new data directory and the keyspace is lost with
nothing reporting a failure.

Relocate the keyspace during activate: mount the DRBD device if it is not
already mounted, restore the snapshot into the fixed member's data
directory, render the environment file to match, then start the member and
verify it serves the restored data before the upgrade proceeds.

The hash check is skipped on restore. The snapshot is taken from a live
member rather than written by snapshot save, so it carries no integrity
hash and etcdutl refuses it without the flag.

Duplex needs no equivalent. There the fixed members join a running cluster
and replicate through raft, so the data arrives without being moved.

Test Plan:
  PASS  simplex upgrade relocates the keyspace to the fixed member's data
        directory and the member serves it
  PASS  keys written before the upgrade read back unchanged after activate
  PASS  a second activate is a no-op
  PASS  duplex upgrade unaffected
