Story: 2010302
Task: 51206
Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/starlingx/stx-puppet/+/998118
Change-Id: Idcd5136ebc6a0ff87ef2895720ced867337749d6
Signed-off-by: bhushan.dhikale <BhushanBhaskar.Dhikale@windriver.com>

usm: relocate etcd keyspace on simplex upgrade

On simplex the etcd keyspace lives on the DRBD-backed path used by the
floating instance. The fixed-first design runs a single local-disk
member instead, so the data has to move before that member starts, or it
founds an empty cluster on the new data directory and the keyspace is
lost with nothing reporting a failure.

Relocate the keyspace during activate: mount the DRBD device if it is
not already mounted, restore the snapshot into the fixed member's data
directory, render the environment file to match, then start the member
and verify it serves the restored data before the upgrade proceeds.

The hash check is skipped on restore. The snapshot is taken from a live
member rather than written by snapshot save, so it carries no integrity
hash and etcdutl refuses it without the flag.

Duplex needs no equivalent. There the fixed members join a running
cluster and replicate through raft, so the data arrives without being
moved.

Both scripts now take their etcdctl command and dial timeouts from
_etcd_common, so the values are defined once. The remaining bounds in
the simplex script are named for what they bound -- systemctl, mount and
a local snapshot restore -- and the health wait keeps its own deadline,
which is a polling bound rather than a command timeout.

Addresses are resolved rather than hardcoded. The duplex script took its
etcdctl endpoint and its certificate SAN check from literal management
addresses, which breaks on any non-default cluster-host subnet and on
every IPv6 deployment, and it built peer URLs without RFC 2732
bracketing.

Test Plan:
  PASS  simplex upgrade relocates the keyspace to the fixed member's data
        directory and the member serves it
  PASS  keys written before the upgrade read back unchanged after activate
  PASS  a second activate is a no-op
  PASS  duplex upgrade unaffected
  PASS  openstack-tox-linters, py3-flake8, py3-bandit
  TODO  duplex activate on an IPv6 cluster-host subnet, to exercise the
        resolved endpoint and the bracketed peer URL

revisions.message:
NetApp ONTAP REST: restore snapshot-dir fallback for CG clones

Restores two code paths dropped when patch 993363 was split to remove
its bug-fix portion:

* nfs_cmode.py stopped passing source_snapshot to clone_file(), so NFS
  CG-snapshot clones silently sourced from the live file instead of
  the snapshot.
* client_cmode_rest.py's clone_lun()/clone_file() lost the
  snapshot_directory_access_enabled check and private-CLI fallback, so
  clones failed outright when that FlexVol setting is False.

Restores get_volume_snapshot_dir_access(), _clone_via_private_cli(),
_clone_lun_via_private_cli(), _check_lun_visible(), the fallback
branching in clone_lun()/clone_file(), and their unit tests.

Verified live on a real ONTAP cluster: iSCSI and NFS CG-snapshot clones
now succeed with snapshot_directory_access_enabled both True and
False, and the NFS clone log shows the real snapshot id instead of
None.

Closes-Bug: #2163623
Depends-On: Ib07d2cd496cdac490313b69e55b03093b012af9d
Change-Id: Ic4946bc7dbd423cd8b8f236c36a975e306dfa914

  clones failed outright when that FlexVol setting is False.

Restores get_volume_snapshot_dir_access(), _clone_via_private_cli(),
_clone_lun_via_private_cli(), the fallback branching in
clone_lun()/clone_file(), and their unit tests.

Also addresses review feedback on the private-CLI fallback: it now
carries is_backup/overwrite_destination (clone_file) and
space_reserved/qos_policy_group_name (clone_lun) through to the CLI
endpoint instead of silently dropping them, and drops the
_check_lun_visible() sanity check, which only logged a warning and
could produce false positives from read-after-write lag.

Verified live on a real ONTAP cluster: iSCSI and NFS CG-snapshot clones
now succeed with snapshot_directory_access_enabled both True and
False, and the NFS clone log shows the real snapshot id instead of
None.

etcd: add certificate reissue and fix member-add guard for SX-to-DX

The simplex-to-duplex migration path fails on the first duplex unlock
because of two issues in the etcd puppet code:

1. Certificate SAN mismatch: At simplex bootstrap the etcd server
   certificate only carries the cluster-host floating address in its
   Subject Alternative Name set. After conversion the membership class
   rewrites etcd-fixed to bind the controller-0 unit address, and the
   TLS handshake fails because the certificate does not cover it.

   Fix: add platform::etcd::certificates, a puppet class that calls
   etcd_duplex_migration.py --certificates to reissue the certificate
   with the full SAN set (floating + both unit addresses + loopback).
   The class is ordered after platform::network writes /etc/hosts and
   before platform::etcd::membership restarts etcd-fixed. An unless
   guard makes it a no-op when the SAN set is already correct (fresh
   duplex bootstrap).

2. Member-add unless guard: The migration playbook registers the
   floating etcd member as a learner before the unlock. At unlock
   puppet tries to add it again. The unless guard greps for the member
   name ('controller'), but an unstarted learner has an empty name
   field in 'etcdctl member list' output -- only the peer URL is
   present. The grep fails, puppet runs the add, etcd returns "Peer
   URLs already exists", and controllerconfig fails.

   Fix: extend the unless guard to also match the floating peer URL
   so it catches both started (by name) and unstarted (by URL) members.

Test Plan:
- AIO-SX to AIO-DX migration with etcd-ha-controlplane topic
- Verified controller-0 boots into duplex mode after unlock
- Verified etcd cluster has 2 members (fixed-0 + controller/floating)
- Verified fresh duplex bootstrap is unaffected (certificates class skips)

revisions.message:
Allow shrinking a segment range to an allocated boundary

Updating a network segment range to reduce its minimum or maximum was
rejected as referenced by a tenant network even when every allocated
segment still fell within the requested new range. The guard against
stranding allocated segments used inclusive comparisons (>= and <=),
so a new boundary that landed exactly on the lowest or highest
allocated segment was wrongly treated as impacting them.

Use strict comparisons so the update is only blocked when the new
minimum rises above the lowest allocated segment or the new maximum
drops below the highest allocated segment.

Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/neutron-tempest-plugin/+/1000364
Closes-Bug: #2161678

revisions.message:
sysinv: apply the control-plane endpoint manifest after unlock

Move controlPlaneEndpoint from the kube-apiserver port onto the HAProxy
load balancer after unlock. Bootstrap points it at kube-apiserver directly
because HAProxy is configured by the unlock manifest and started by Service
Manager, so nothing listens on :6443 while kubeadm init runs.

Apply it from iplatform_update_by_ihost() on the first-report-available
path, immediately after the etcd runtime manifest. The same guards apply:
controller personality, non-simplex, initial config complete.

This also covers the other lifecycle paths without a separate hook:
- simplex-to-duplex: the script returns early on simplex, picks up on
  the first unlock as duplex
- upgrade/rollback: each unlock re-applies, no-op when already correct
- restore: reconciles from whatever the backup captured

Depends-On: I91726856fd800f9c5de5277ec4a5dcfb2b5be216
Change-Id: I5c3b5d99545e2b3033d96aa3cd11e160845291b7

Test Plan:

Remove disabling the scope enforcement

RBAC scope enforcement was controlled by the oslo.policy
deprecated config option enforce_scope which has been removed
in oslo.policy 6.0.0. That removes the ability to disable
the scope enforcement which is the end goal of SRBAC.

- https://governance.openstack.org/tc/goals/selected/consistent-and-secure-rbac.html#id5

Adding upgrade impact in releasenotes with olso.policy version
bump in requirements.txt.

revisions.message:
Support multiple external sources in synce4l

The sysinv puppet networking module stored external_source as a
single dict per synce4l instance. When multiple ptp-interfaces
had external_source configured, only the last one survived
(overwrite). This prevented configuring GNSS vs SyncE priority
selection via internal_prio on E825 hardware.

Change instance['external_source'] (dict) to
instance['external_sources'] (list) and append each result from
_set_external_source_parameters() instead of overwriting.

Add port section deduplication for synce4l instances: when
multiple ptp-interfaces share the same physical port, merge
their parameters into a single [port] section to avoid invalid
duplicate sections in the generated config file. This is scoped
to synce4l only — other instance types are unaffected.

Test Plan:

      port produce single [port] section and two [{ext_src}]
      sections with correct independent parameters

revisions.message:
Derive versionCode/versionName from git at build time

versionCode/versionName were frozen at 1/"1.0.0", which made every
sideload indistinguishable from the last -- this cost a diagnosis
day during the API-host outage, when "which build is on the phone"
had no answer. A frozen versionCode also blocks Google Play, which
rejects any upload whose versionCode is not strictly greater than
the last.

versionCode is `git rev-list --count HEAD`: it only grows as commits
land, so it is monotonic along any branch's history, merge commits
included. This depends on a full clone -- verified, not assumed,
that Zuul checks out this repo without shallow-clone: no such config
exists in .zuul.yaml, the playbooks, or system-config, and Zuul's
merger needs full history anyway for speculative cross-repo merges.
A non-master branch/patchset build can produce a count that does not
follow monotonically after master's own sequence; that is fine,
because those builds are check/gate builds that are never published
to Play.

versionName is BASE_VERSION-<count>-g<shortsha>. No tags exist yet,
so BASE_VERSION is a named constant standing in for a future
`git describe`-based scheme once release tagging starts.

A build with no git metadata (e.g. a source tarball) falls back to
versionCode 1 / versionName "<BASE_VERSION>-nogit" with a
logger.warn, rather than failing outright.

Git's output is captured through a ValueSource-backed provider
(GitCommandValueSource) instead of a bare exec() call in the script
body, which is the configuration-cache-safe way to shell out from a
build script on Gradle 8.5. There is no buildSrc module in this
repo, so it lives as a top-level class in app/build.gradle.kts.

SettingsScreen's "WanderTracks v1.0.0" label now reads
BuildConfig.VERSION_NAME instead of a hardcoded string -- buildConfig
generation was already on, the field just was not being used. Its
instrumented test assertion is updated the same way, since the
string it checks for is no longer a fixed literal.

Signing, build types and Play publishing plumbing are untouched --
this is version stamping only, useful for sideload diagnostics on
its own regardless of Play.

revisions.message:
Wait for power state in baremetal functional tests

set_node_power_state() is asynchronous: the bare metal API returns 202
as soon as ironic acknowledges the request, before the conductor has
committed the new power state to the database. Several functional
tests called it without wait=True and then immediately performed an
operation that depends on the power state having landed.

For the allocation tests this caused intermittent failures. The shared
setUp forces a power off so that the node has a non-empty power state
-- fake-hardware never populates one on its own -- because allocation
candidate selection filters on power_state IS NOT NULL. When the
allocation was created inside the window between the 202 and the
conductor's write, no candidate matched and the allocation failed with
"no available nodes match the resource class". In one observed run the
conductor committed the power state 20ms after the allocation had
already been rejected.

The volume connector and volume target tests share the same pattern,
where ironic requires the node to be powered off before a volume
connector or target can be updated.

Add wait=True to every set_node_power_state() call in the bare metal
functional tests. The set_node_provision_state() calls already all
pass wait=True.

Closes-bug: #2164899
Assisted-by: Claude-code (opus 5)
Change-Id: Icc947903043a5cccc79d19ef501295128982c33d
Signed-off-by: Jay Faulkner <jay@jvf.cc>

subject: Wait for power state in baremetal functional tests

revisions.message:
Add OpenStack PVC backup and restore to app-owned playbooks

The application-owned backup and restore playbooks (introduced in
Ibd73b6bf) do not handle OpenStack PVC data for services that use
Kubernetes PersistentVolumeClaims as their storage backend. After a
restore, MariaDB references data that no longer exists in the
recreated PVCs, causing images, backups, and ephemeral instances to
become non-functional.

Add OpenStack PVC backup and restore by creating Kubernetes
VolumeSnapshots during backup (capturing the snapshot handle, storage
class, and PVC metadata into pvc_info.yml included in the backup
tarball) and restoring them before application apply by recreating
the VolumeSnapshotContent, VolumeSnapshot, and PVC with dataSource
pointing to the snapshot. OpenStack PVCs are discovered dynamically
via the helm.sh/resource-policy=keep annotation in the openstack
namespace. If a PVC already exists and is Bound at restore time, it
is skipped. If pvc_info.yml is absent from the backup tarball, the
restore gracefully skips the PVC restore step.

This is the application-owned counterpart of Change-Id
Ib424b1e9cb3aded38c260ec3ec6649de2a31b8f4 (merged in
starlingx/ansible-playbooks). Both changes coexist for 26.10; the
platform copy will be removed when the delegation is complete.

Test Plan:

Validated via the platform-side change (same logic, same test
results). See Ib424b1e9cb3aded38c260ec3ec6649de2a31b8f4 for full
validation including:

[PASS] ISO build with patched playbookconfig package
[PASS] Fresh install from ISO + bootstrap + unlock controller-0
[PASS] Backup captures VolumeSnapshots for all OpenStack PVCs
[PASS] Restore recreates OpenStack PVCs from snapshots
[PASS] Restored Glance image is functional
[PASS] Restored Cinder backup is functional
[PASS] Nova instances PVC is functional

revisions.message:
Build a signed AAB for the first Play upload

Google will not let the Play Developer API create an app's first
release. The listing and the first bundle are a Console act; the API
only operates on an app that already exists. So the bootstrap upload
has to be a file in Monty's hands -- and nothing in this repo produces
one.

wandertracks-android-build-release builds *unsigned*, deliberately: it
runs in vouched and gate, and Zuul refuses an untrusted project's
secrets in pre-review pipelines, so it has no keystore.
wandertracks-android-publish-internal can sign, but it is held out of
every pipeline until the Console setup that requires the very artifact
it would produce. Neither end of that circle can move first.

This adds wandertracks-android-build-release-signed, which breaks it:
build the release bundle signed with the upload key, prove the
signature, publish the bundle as a Zuul artifact, and never speak to
Google Play.

Promote, for the same reason the toolchain image promote is there:
post-review pipelines are the only place Zuul permits this project's
secrets, because they are the only ones that never run unreviewed
code. Not release -- that would make the bootstrap wait on a tag push,
and tag semantics belong to the phase 2 production path. Not post,
which fires at the same moment while adding a pipeline this project
does not otherwise use. Promote also builds the merged commit, so the
git-derived versionCode is a real master versionCode; Play requires
every later upload to exceed the first, and a versionCode from a
speculative gate state would be a bad number to pin the app's history
to.

Enablement is not held. This job is added to the promote pipeline in
the same change that defines it, because unlike the publish job it
depends on nothing of Monty's: one secret,
wandertracks-android-play-signing, which change 1002203 already
carries. Emphatically not wandertracks-android-play-oidc --
independence from Play is the entire value, and this has to work
before a Console account, a Cloud project, a service account or a
workload identity pool exists. Merging the stack is the trigger.

Signing is verified in the job rather than assumed. Setting the two
WANDERTRACKS_UPLOAD_* variables is not evidence that the signing
config took: app/build.gradle.kts builds unsigned when they are
absent, which is exactly the graceful degradation the other jobs rely
on, and a silently-unsigned bundle is rejected by Play with an error
that names nothing useful. So jarsigner -verify -verbose -certs runs
on the staged artifact, and keytool -printcert -jarfile reads the
signer's SHA-256 fingerprint -- the value Play pins as the upload
certificate at the first upload and checks on every upload after.
Both the fingerprint and the full certificate ship as a second
artifact next to the bundle, so the comparison against Play Console
does not depend on a log that ages out. jarsigner rather than
apksigner because an App Bundle is a JAR-signed zip and apksigner
only understands APKs; without -strict, because the upload
certificate is self-signed by design and -strict would fail on that.

The keystore handling is shared, not copied. tasks/upload-keystore.yaml
and tasks/remove-upload-keystore.yaml hold what both playbooks do
identically -- base64 transport, binary-safe decode, the 0600 env file
that keeps a secret out of a task environment so no task needs no_log,
and the always-clause scrub -- and publish-internal.yaml is rewritten
to include them. Included as task files with an explicit
{{ playbook_dir }} path rather than as a role: this repo has no roles/
directory, Zuul's implicit role path is one more thing to be wrong
about, and this job's first real run happens post-merge, which is a
poor place to discover a path assumption. The Play-specific half --
the OIDC token, the credential config -- stays in the publish
playbook, so neither playbook is a maze of conditionals.

It stays after the bootstrap. publish-internal only exercises signing
at the moment it also needs Play reachable, so a signing regression
and a Play outage would arrive as the same red job. This separates
them, and leaves a signed, sideloadable bundle on every master merge.

The doc/plans/play-store-publishing.md section these comments cite is
added by a separate change on top of the plan rewrite (1002204),
since that change rewrites the same file wholesale.

Nothing here can be exercised before it runs for real: promote only
fires post-merge. The Gradle half is already green --
wandertracks-android-build-release passed on 1002209 with the signing
config and GPP applied, which is what proves the unsigned path still
degrades gracefully.

revisions.message:
Promote the bundle the gate signed

Moves wandertracks-android-build-release-signed from promote to gate,
and makes wandertracks-android-publish-internal fetch that build's
bundle instead of building its own.

The design this replaces rested on a false premise. Both jobs were put
in promote because "Zuul permits a project's secrets only in
post-review pipelines, and vouched and gate are pre-review". The
second half is wrong. Checked rather than argued: the config project
this repo's tenant uses is opendev/project-config, whose
zuul.d/pipelines.yaml sets post-review: True on gate and promote and
leaves it unset -- false -- on check and vouched. This repo already
depends on that, and has since before any of this: wandertracks-
upload-android-toolchain-image runs in gate and carries the
wandertracks-android-registry-credentials secret.

With that corrected, the house pattern applies unchanged, and it is
the one the image trio already implements here: build in vouched,
build-and-upload-with-credentials in gate, retag in promote. The
principle is promoting the exact artifact that was tested. A promote
job that rebuilds is shipping something no job ever gated and trusting
that it matches what was; the whole reason OpenDev's image jobs push
to an intermediate registry from gate and only retag afterwards is to
never have to make that assumption. OpenDev's promote pipeline says as
much in its own definition: it "runs jobs that operate after each
change is merged in order to promote artifacts generated in the gate
pipeline".

So:

  vouched   wandertracks-android-build-release        unsigned bundle
  gate      wandertracks-android-build-release-signed signed bundle,
                                                      published as a
                                                      Zuul artifact
  promote   wandertracks-android-publish-internal     fetches it,
                                                      uploads to Play

The signed job replaces the unsigned one in gate rather than running
beside it, the same way the upload image job replaces the build image
job there. Both run the same bundleRelease; the signed one also signs
and verifies, so running both would buy a second R8 pass and nothing
else. The unsigned job stays in vouched, where secrets are unavailable
and where it goes on proving that app/build.gradle.kts still degrades
to an unsigned bundle with no keystore present -- the degradation
every developer build depends on.

How the bundle crosses the pipeline boundary, which is the part worth
checking rather than inventing: zuul-jobs' download-artifact role,
which OpenDev's own base-jobs uses for non-image artifacts --
playbooks/docs/promote.yaml and playbooks/artifacts/promote.yaml both
run it with download_artifact_pipeline: gate. Its default query is
change, patchset, pipeline and job_name. A promote item is a Gerrit
change-merged event, so zuul.change and zuul.patchset hold the change
that just merged, the same pair the gate build was recorded under.
Verified against the live API, not assumed: a promote build of this
project reports ref.change and ref.patchset, and querying
/api/tenant/opendev/builds with that change, patchset, pipeline=gate
and a job name returns the gate build with its artifact URLs intact.
The log store keeps those for roughly a month; promote runs seconds
after the gate that produced them.

Unlike base-jobs' promote playbooks the download runs on the node, not
the executor. Those jobs are node-less and push to AFS from the
executor; this one needs the file where Gradle can read it, so
fetching to the executor would only add a hop. Promote does take a
nodeset for that -- permitted, and not theoretical: the opendev tenant
already runs drizzle-publish-nox-docs on a node in promote, and the
openstack tenant runs the openstack-helm-images-promote-* jobs there.

Uploading a pre-built artifact is GPP's own supported mode, not a
trick: --artifact-dir. With artifactDir set, PlayPublisherPlugin
resolves the publish task's artifact dependency to nothing, so no
bundleRelease runs -- which is also why the publish job no longer
takes the signing secret at all. wandertracks-android-play-signing
stays with the job that signs; the only credential in promote is the
keyless OIDC token. Verified by reading PlayPublisherPlugin.kt and
CliOptions.kt at 3.13.0, not the README.

The empty-directory case gets an explicit assertion, because GPP marks
the publish task's bundle input @SkipWhenEmpty: pointing it at a
directory with no .aab in it skips the task and reports success having
uploaded nothing. The role fails loudly when the API returns no gate
build, but an artifact whose metadata type stopped matching would
arrive as an empty directory, so the file count is checked before
Gradle is invoked. The directory is removed and recreated first, since
GPP uploads every artifact it finds there.

The bootstrap property is intact and slightly better. The signed build
still needs only wandertracks-android-play-signing -- never the OIDC
secret, never a Play Console account, a Cloud project, a service
account or a workload identity pool -- because it never contacts
Google. In gate it now produces that bundle on every approved change
rather than only on merges, so the first signed AAB is available from
the gate run of this very change.

Two consequences of gating the artifact instead of rebuilding it, both
accepted rather than engineered around:

The bundle's git-derived versionCode comes from Zuul's speculative
merge state rather than from the merge commit Gerrit writes. The tree
is identical -- that is what the gate tested -- but `git rev-list
--count HEAD` can differ by one from the post-merge count. It does not
matter: Play requires each upload's versionCode to exceed the previous
one, not to equal any particular number, and a count taken from a
speculative merge still rises strictly with every subsequent one,
since master only grows underneath it.

GPP's releaseName comes from the versionName computed on the promote
node from the merged commit, while the bundle's embedded versionCode
was computed in the gate. The two can disagree by that same commit's
worth of count. It affects only the label shown against the release in
Play Console; nothing keys off it. Carrying the version through
artifact metadata and passing --release-name would fix it, and is not
worth the coupling until the label actually misleads someone.

The shared keystore task files go away with this. They existed because
two playbooks materialized the keystore; now only one does, so
playbooks/tasks/ would be indirection for a single caller, and the
handling is inline in playbooks/build-signed-bundle.yaml.

There is no Android SDK on the machine this was written on, and none
of the publish path can be exercised before it runs for real: promote
only fires post-merge and the OIDC exchange hits live Google
endpoints. What this change's own gate does exercise is the signing
job in its new pipeline, which is the half that has to work first.
